subtopic_detail: Discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks and 4 days. Chorionicity was established at the 11 week scan by the T sign and a single placental mass.

She reports increasing abdominal tightness and breathlessness over ten days. Today's scan shows twin one with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm and a bladder that is not visualised over 40 minutes of observation, and twin two with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm and a full bladder. Both twins have normal umbilical artery Doppler waveforms with positive end diastolic flow and normal ductus venosus waveforms. Neither twin is hydropic and the estimated foetal weights differ by 14 per cent. Her cervical length is 34 mm and she is not contracting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with bladder not visualised; twin two deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with full bladder; umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers normal in both; cervical length 34 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks as part of the standard monochorionic surveillance schedule
options.rationale: Two weekly surveillance is for a normal monochorionic pregnancy, and a fortnight of observation once the sequence is established carries a very high risk of double foetal loss (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Urgent referral to a foetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
options.rationale: Deepest vertical pockets below 2 cm and above 8 cm in a monochorionic diamniotic pair with an absent bladder in the donor establish the diagnosis at stage two, where laser ablation of the placental anastomoses is the treatment that improves survival before 26 weeks (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac with repeat drainage as maternal symptoms recur
options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves maternal symptoms and reduces preterm labour risk but does not treat the underlying vascular anastomoses, and it gives worse survival and neurological outcomes than laser (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Delivery by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids has been completed
options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is below the threshold of viability and would result in the loss of both twins, whereas intrauterine treatment offers a realistic chance of survival (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the co twin from injury
options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for advanced disease with an unsalvageable twin or where laser is not feasible, and Dopplers here remain normal in both twins (Source: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates about 10 to 15 per cent of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies through unbalanced flow across placental vascular anastomoses. Diagnosis requires monochorionicity plus discordant amniotic fluid, defined in Australian practice as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other, and growth discordance is neither necessary nor sufficient. The Quintero staging system runs from stage one, with discordant fluid alone, through absent donor bladder at stage two, abnormal Dopplers at stage three, hydrops at stage four and demise at stage five. Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation is the treatment of choice before 26 weeks because it addresses the anastomoses rather than the fluid, and it is why chorionicity must be established in the first trimester and surveillance run fortnightly from 16 weeks.
key_points: Diagnosis needs monochorionicity plus a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm and above 8 cm
An absent donor bladder defines Quintero stage two
Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation is first line before 26 weeks
Amnioreduction treats symptoms but not the underlying anastomoses
explanation.pearls: Growth discordance alone does not diagnose twin to twin transfusion syndrome; selective foetal growth restriction in a monochorionic pair has normal amniotic fluid in both sacs and is managed with Doppler surveillance rather than laser.

sources.label: RANZCOG Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy Guideline
Australasian Society for Ultrasound in Medicine twin guidance

subtopic_detail: Acute scrotal pain with coexisting urinary symptoms in an adolescent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 14 year old boy who developed severe left scrotal pain five hours ago while sitting in class. He vomited twice on the way to hospital and has not been able to walk comfortably.

He reports stinging when passing urine over the last three days and his urine dipstick today shows leucocytes and nitrites. On examination the left testis sits higher than the right and lies transversely, the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left and present on the right, and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. There is no scrotal erythema or fixed swelling and he is afebrile. Ultrasound is available but the sonographer is 45 minutes away from the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 122/70, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse; cremasteric reflex absent on the left, present on the right; Prehn sign negative; no scrotal erythema
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucocytes and nitrites positive; urine culture sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim with analgesia and outpatient urology review once the urine culture returns
options.rationale: Treating the urinary findings as the whole explanation ignores the high riding transverse lie and absent cremasteric reflex, and a coexisting urinary infection does not exclude torsion (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and surgical referral only if arterial flow is reduced
options.rationale: Imaging that delays exploration is the classic anti pattern here, and Doppler can show preserved flow in incomplete or intermittent torsion, producing false reassurance (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Manual detorsion at the bedside with analgesia and discharge home if the pain settles completely
options.rationale: Manual detorsion is a temporising manoeuvre while theatre is prepared and never replaces exploration, since it frequently leaves residual twist and does not fix the underlying anatomy (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

options.text: Immediate urological referral for scrotal exploration with fixation of both testes if confirmed
options.rationale: Sudden severe pain with a high riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex is torsion until proven otherwise, and exploration within six hours of onset gives the best salvage rate, so it proceeds without imaging (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain; Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance).
source_refs: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with admission for observation and reassessment by the surgical team overnight
options.rationale: Overnight observation spends the salvage window, since testicular viability falls sharply beyond six hours and is largely lost by twelve (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Scrotal Pain).

explanation.summary: Testicular torsion is a time critical diagnosis where salvage rates exceed 90 per cent within six hours, fall to around 50 per cent by twelve hours and approach zero beyond twenty four. The diagnosis is clinical, and the features that matter most are sudden severe onset, a high riding or transverse testis, an absent cremasteric reflex and pain unrelieved by elevation. Ultrasound has meaningful false negative rates in incomplete or intermittent torsion and its main role is in equivocal cases where it will not delay theatre. A coexisting urinary tract infection or epididymo-orchitis does not exclude torsion, and the presence of a plausible alternative diagnosis is one of the commonest reasons torsion is missed in adolescents.
key_points: Salvage exceeds 90 per cent within six hours and falls steeply thereafter
Absent cremasteric reflex and a high riding transverse testis are the strongest clinical signs
Doppler ultrasound can be falsely reassuring in incomplete or intermittent torsion
A coexisting urinary infection does not exclude torsion in an adolescent
explanation.pearls: Both testes are fixed at exploration because the bell clapper deformity that permits torsion is bilateral in most affected boys, so fixing only the affected side leaves a substantial risk of contralateral torsion later.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand guidance

subtopic_detail: Initial approach to a request for gender affirming hormone therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old trans man who has lived in his affirmed gender for three years, uses he and him pronouns at work and with family, and has had a legal name change. He requests testosterone therapy.

He describes persistent distress about chest and menstrual bleeding, and says this has been consistent since age 13. He has no psychotic symptoms, substance use, self harm or suicidal ideation. He works full time and has supportive parents. He has not previously seen a psychiatrist and asks whether a psychiatric assessment is required before he can start. His blood pressure and body mass index are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, engaged, no psychotic features, no cognitive impairment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Require twelve months of psychiatric assessment before any hormone therapy can be considered
options.rationale: A mandatory extended psychiatric gatekeeping period is not part of current Australian practice and is associated with delayed care and worse mental health outcomes (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Commence testosterone undecanoate today and arrange follow up bloods in three months
options.rationale: Baseline haematocrit, lipids and liver function are needed before starting, since erythrocytosis is the commonest dose limiting adverse effect and cannot be interpreted without a pretreatment value (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Commence sertraline for the reported distress and revisit hormone therapy after three months
options.rationale: The distress described is gender dysphoria rather than a depressive disorder, and an antidepressant neither treats it nor is a prerequisite for hormone therapy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer to a public gender clinic and take no further action until that appointment occurs
options.rationale: Referral alone with waiting times often exceeding a year leaves the patient without care and without the baseline investigations that any prescriber will need at the first appointment (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Arrange baseline haematocrit, lipids and liver function and discuss fertility preservation options
options.rationale: Australian informed consent practice for an adult with sustained gender incongruence and capacity is baseline biochemistry plus documented discussion of fertility, reversibility and expected effects, after which a general practitioner may initiate or co manage therapy (Source: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy).
source_refs: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Australian practice for adults has moved from a psychiatric gatekeeping model to an informed consent model, in which the prescriber confirms capacity, sustained gender incongruence and understanding of effects, then initiates therapy with appropriate monitoring. Mental health assessment remains relevant where a condition might impair capacity or where comorbidity needs treatment in its own right, but it is not a universal prerequisite. Fertility discussion must occur before starting, because testosterone reduces fertility and oocyte cryopreservation is far simpler before treatment begins. Ongoing monitoring focuses on haematocrit, lipids, liver function and blood pressure, with dose adjusted to symptom response and testosterone level.
key_points: Informed consent, not mandatory psychiatric clearance, is the Australian adult standard
Baseline haematocrit, lipids, liver function and blood pressure precede initiation
Fertility preservation is discussed and documented before therapy starts
Erythrocytosis is the commonest dose limiting adverse effect of testosterone therapy
explanation.pearls: Monitor haematocrit at three, six and twelve months then annually on testosterone; a haematocrit above 0.54 requires dose reduction or a switch to a lower peak formulation rather than simple reassurance.

sources.label: Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

subtopic_detail: Cortisol testing confounded by oestrogen containing contraception
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman referred with weight gain, purple abdominal striae wider than one centimetre, proximal muscle weakness on standing from a chair, and new hypertension at 152/96 mmHg.

She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol and has done so continuously for four years. She takes no corticosteroid in any form, including inhaled, topical and intra articular preparations, and drinks no alcohol. Her general practitioner performed a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test which returned a morning cortisol of 78 nmol/L, above the suppression threshold of 50 nmol/L. Her potassium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 152/96, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test: morning cortisol 78 nmol/L (suppression threshold below 50); potassium and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Purple abdominal striae greater than 1 cm wide; proximal weakness on sit to stand testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary to identify a corticotroph adenoma
options.rationale: Imaging before the biochemical diagnosis is secure risks acting on an incidental pituitary lesion, which is present in around one in ten of the population (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone now to determine whether the excess is dependent
options.rationale: Determining dependence is the correct second stage but only after hypercortisolism is confirmed, and the current result cannot confirm it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Repeat the same overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test in six weeks for confirmation
options.rationale: Repeating the identical test while the confounder continues will reproduce the same uninterpretable result, since the problem is assay interference rather than random variation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of the cortisol excess
options.rationale: Petrosal sinus sampling is an invasive tertiary test used to separate pituitary from ectopic sources long after confirmation of hypercortisolism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections while she continues the pill
options.rationale: Oestrogen raises cortisol binding globulin and therefore total serum cortisol, producing false non suppression, whereas urinary free cortisol measures unbound hormone and is unaffected by binding globulin (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Screening for Cushing syndrome uses three first line tests, the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24 hour urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol, and at least two abnormal results are needed before proceeding. Oestrogen containing preparations raise cortisol binding globulin by roughly 50 per cent, which inflates total serum cortisol and causes apparent failure of dexamethasone suppression in healthy women. The alternatives are to cease oestrogen for six weeks and repeat the suppression test, or to use a test that measures free rather than total cortisol. Other important confounders are enzyme inducing drugs such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin, which accelerate dexamethasone metabolism and also cause false non suppression.
key_points: Oestrogen raises cortisol binding globulin and inflates total serum cortisol
Urinary free cortisol and late night salivary cortisol measure free hormone and avoid this confounder
Two abnormal first line tests are required before proceeding to determine dependence
Enzyme inducing anticonvulsants and rifampicin also cause false non suppression
explanation.pearls: If a suppression test is to be repeated off oestrogen, six weeks of cessation is required for cortisol binding globulin to normalise; four weeks is a common shortcut that still leaves the result uninterpretable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

subtopic_detail: Timing of thromboprophylaxis after neuraxial anaesthesia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36 year old woman two hours after an emergency caesarean section performed for failure to progress at full dilatation. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she had an unprovoked pulmonary embolism at age 28 that was treated for six months.

The caesarean was performed under a top up of her labour epidural, and the epidural catheter is still in situ for postoperative analgesia. The anaesthetist plans to remove it once she is mobile this evening, roughly six hours from now. Estimated blood loss was 700 mL, her uterus is well contracted and her lochia is normal. Her platelet count is 214 x10^9/L, her coagulation screen is within normal limits and she has no ongoing bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted at the umbilicus, lochia normal, epidural catheter in situ and functioning
data_table.Blood tests: Platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400); coagulation screen within normal limits; haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin starting now and continuing for ten days after the caesarean section
options.rationale: Two errors compound here: giving low molecular weight heparin with an epidural catheter in situ risks spinal haematoma, and ten days is too short for a prior unprovoked event (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

options.text: Graduated compression stockings and early mobilisation with no pharmacological prophylaxis given
options.rationale: Mechanical measures alone are inadequate for a woman with a previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism, obesity and operative delivery, which is a high risk combination (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

options.text: Low dose aspirin daily for six weeks with graduated compression stockings while an inpatient
options.rationale: Aspirin is an antiplatelet used for preeclampsia prophylaxis in pregnancy and is not adequate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in this risk group (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin starting four hours after epidural catheter removal and continuing six weeks
options.rationale: A prior unprovoked event warrants six weeks of postpartum prophylaxis, and the first dose is withheld until at least four hours after catheter removal to avoid epidural haematoma (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline; ANZCA neuraxial anticoagulation guidance).
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

options.text: Therapeutic dose enoxaparin starting after catheter removal and continuing for three months postpartum
options.rationale: Treatment dose anticoagulation is for an acute thrombosis rather than prophylaxis after a remote event, and it raises the risk of postpartum haemorrhage and wound haematoma unnecessarily (Source: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the postpartum period carries the highest daily risk of the whole pregnancy. Risk assessment is repeated at booking, on any antenatal admission and after birth, with prophylaxis duration set by the risk category rather than by length of stay. Ten days covers moderate risk after caesarean section, whereas a previous unprovoked or oestrogen related event, thrombophilia with a family history, or several persisting risk factors warrant six weeks. Neuraxial anaesthesia adds a timing constraint that is independent of the risk calculation, requiring at least four hours between catheter removal and a prophylactic dose, and at least 12 hours between a prophylactic dose and catheter removal.
key_points: Postpartum risk assessment sets the duration: ten days for moderate risk, six weeks for high risk
A previous unprovoked event places a woman in the six week category
Wait at least four hours after epidural catheter removal before a prophylactic heparin dose
Wait at least twelve hours after a prophylactic dose before removing a catheter
explanation.pearls: Enoxaparin prophylaxis is dosed by booking weight, so a woman above 90 kg needs 40 mg twice daily rather than the standard once daily dose; fixed dosing regardless of weight is the commonest prophylaxis failure in obese postpartum women.

sources.label: RANZCOG Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Pregnancy and the Puerperium Guideline

subtopic_detail: Late presentation of a duct dependent systemic circulation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 6 day old term baby girl. Her mother says she has gone off her feeds since yesterday, is breathing fast, and looked grey and mottled this morning.

She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with no antenatal concerns and was discharged at 36 hours of age. On examination she is pale and mottled with cool legs. Her right brachial pulse is easily palpable but both femoral pulses are impalpable. Pre-ductal saturation in the right hand is 96 per cent and post-ductal saturation in the right foot is 88 per cent. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.18 with a lactate of 7.4 mmol/L and her blood glucose is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 62/34 right arm, RR 66, SpO2 96% right hand and 88% right foot, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Pale and mottled with cool legs; right brachial pulse present, both femoral pulses impalpable; liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18 (7.32-7.42); lactate 7.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L (2.6-6.0); chest radiograph cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
options.rationale: Sepsis is the correct parallel consideration and antibiotics should be given, but a large fluid bolus alone worsens pulmonary congestion here and leaves the duct closing (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intubation with hyperventilation and high flow oxygen to correct the metabolic acidosis rapidly
options.rationale: High inspired oxygen and hypocapnia both reduce pulmonary vascular resistance, which diverts more blood into the lungs and further reduces systemic perfusion in a duct dependent systemic circulation (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to restore blood pressure and peripheral perfusion
options.rationale: Inotropes may be needed as an adjunct but they cannot restore lower body flow while the arterial duct is closing, which is the mechanical problem to be reversed (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Urgent echocardiography to define the anatomy before commencing any cardiovascular treatment
options.rationale: Waiting for imaging is the near pair error, since the pre and post ductal saturation gradient with absent femoral pulses is already sufficient to act and the duct may close within hours (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

options.text: Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion with antibiotics and preparation for intubation and transfer
options.rationale: A pre to post ductal saturation gradient with impalpable femoral pulses and lactic acidosis at day 6 indicates a duct dependent systemic circulation, and prostaglandin reopens the duct while antibiotics cover the sepsis that cannot yet be excluded (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

explanation.summary: Duct dependent systemic lesions such as coarctation, interrupted aortic arch, critical aortic stenosis and hypoplastic left heart present in the first two weeks as the arterial duct closes, and they are frequently mistaken for sepsis because both produce a shocked, mottled, tachypnoeic neonate. The findings that separate them are a pre to post ductal saturation gradient greater than 3 per cent, absent or weak femoral pulses, and a lactic acidosis out of proportion to the respiratory findings. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and is started on clinical suspicion rather than after echocardiography, because the duct can close completely within hours. Apnoea is the main adverse effect and occurs in around 10 to 12 per cent, so the airway plan is made at the same time as the infusion is started.
key_points: A pre to post ductal saturation gradient above 3 per cent with weak femoral pulses points to a duct dependent systemic lesion
Prostaglandin E1 is started on clinical grounds without waiting for echocardiography
High inspired oxygen worsens systemic perfusion by lowering pulmonary vascular resistance
Give antibiotics in parallel, since sepsis cannot be excluded at the bedside
explanation.pearls: Apnoea complicates prostaglandin E1 infusion in roughly one in ten neonates and is dose related, so airway equipment and an intubation plan must be at the cot side before the infusion starts, particularly for a road or air transfer.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Neonate

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening and hypotension
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 22 year old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking an unknown quantity of her grandmother's amitriptyline. She was drowsy on arrival and has become progressively less responsive over the last ten minutes.

She had one self limiting generalised seizure in the ambulance. She takes no other medication and there is no alcohol detected. Intravenous access is established and she is being preoxygenated with a plan for intubation. Her serial electrocardiograms show a progressively widening QRS complex and a rightward terminal axis in lead aVR. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.22 with a bicarbonate of 15 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 82/48, RR 26, SpO2 97% on 15 L oxygen, temperature 36.4
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 152 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm; venous pH 7.22 (7.32-7.42); bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Blood tests: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); paracetamol not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading infusion to prevent recurrence of the seizure
options.rationale: Phenytoin is a sodium channel blocker itself and worsens cardiotoxicity in this poisoning; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over twenty minutes for the broad complex tachycardia
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic and class III antiarrhythmics all worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated, which is the key difference from a primary ventricular tachycardia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Intravenous noradrenaline infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Vasopressors have a role once sodium loading and alkalinisation have been given, but starting with noradrenaline leaves the sodium channel blockade itself untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol by rapid bolus with repeat boluses guided by the QRS
options.rationale: Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate reverses tricyclic sodium channel blockade by both sodium loading and alkalinisation, and is indicated for a QRS above 100 ms, seizures or hypotension in this poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; NSW Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 per cent given as a bolus then infusion over thirty minutes
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy considered only in cardiac arrest or refractory collapse after bicarbonate has failed, not as the first line intervention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning kills through fast sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia and myocardial depression, compounded by alpha blockade and antimuscarinic effects. The electrocardiogram is the main severity tool, with a QRS above 100 ms predicting seizures and above 160 ms predicting ventricular arrhythmia, and a terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm supporting the diagnosis. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate works through two mechanisms at once and is titrated against the QRS duration rather than against a fixed dose. Acidosis from seizure or hypoventilation worsens toxicity, so airway control with adequate ventilation is part of the treatment rather than a separate issue.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures; above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia
Sodium bicarbonate is titrated to QRS narrowing, not to a fixed total dose
Phenytoin, amiodarone and other sodium channel blocking antiarrhythmics are contraindicated
Benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice in this poisoning
explanation.pearls: Aim for a serum pH of 7.50 to 7.55 during bicarbonate therapy for tricyclic toxicity and recheck the QRS after each 100 mmol bolus; a QRS that stops narrowing despite target pH signals the need for vasopressor support.

subtopic_detail: Interfering antihypertensives in aldosterone to renin ratio testing
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the hypertension clinic seeing a 44 year old woman whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite three agents at maximum tolerated doses. She has been on perindopril, amlodipine and spironolactone for the last five months.

Her potassium has been persistently low at 3.1 mmol/L on three occasions and she takes no diuretic other than the spironolactone and no liquorice or over the counter preparations. Her renal function and thyroid function are within normal limits, her urinary metanephrines are not raised and a renal artery duplex shows no stenosis. Her general practitioner has sent an aldosterone to renin ratio which came back below the screening threshold. She asks why her potassium keeps dropping.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 168/102, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Investigations: Aldosterone to renin ratio below screening threshold; urinary metanephrines not raised; renal artery duplex no stenosis
data_table.Blood tests: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); sodium 142 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease spironolactone for six weeks, substitute verapamil and prazosin, then repeat the ratio
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists raise renin and suppress the aldosterone to renin ratio, producing false negatives, so they must be withdrawn for at least six weeks with blood pressure covered by agents that do not interfere (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Accept the negative ratio and add a fourth agent such as hydralazine to control the pressure
options.rationale: Accepting an uninterpretable result leaves a potentially curable cause unexamined in a patient with the classic combination of resistant hypertension and spontaneous hypokalaemia (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to lateralise aldosterone production before any imaging
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling is a lateralisation test performed after biochemical confirmation, and doing it first exposes the patient to an invasive procedure without an established diagnosis (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the adrenal glands and act on any adenoma that is identified
options.rationale: Non functioning adrenal incidentalomas are common and acting on imaging without biochemical confirmation leads to inappropriate adrenalectomy (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

options.text: Perform a saline suppression test now while the current antihypertensive regimen is continued
options.rationale: The saline suppression test is the near pair confirmatory step, but it is invalidated by exactly the same drug interference that invalidated the screening ratio (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest secondary cause of hypertension and is substantially underdiagnosed, largely because screening tests are performed on drugs that invalidate them. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone and eplerenone raise renin and produce false negative ratios, and beta blockers do the reverse by suppressing renin and producing false positives. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics all interfere to a lesser degree, whereas verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine and moxonidine are considered ratio neutral. Confirming the diagnosis matters because unilateral disease can be cured surgically and bilateral disease is treated with a targeted mineralocorticoid antagonist rather than escalating generic therapy.
key_points: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia should always prompt screening
Spironolactone and eplerenone cause false negatives and need six weeks of withdrawal
Beta blockers cause false positives by suppressing renin
Verapamil, prazosin, hydralazine and moxonidine are ratio neutral cover during washout
explanation.pearls: Correct hypokalaemia to above 4.0 mmol/L before sampling for an aldosterone to renin ratio, because potassium depletion suppresses aldosterone secretion and can mask the diagnosis it is supposed to reveal.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia clinical guidance

subtopic_detail: Antithrombotic management in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome
stem:
You are the registrar in the recurrent miscarriage clinic seeing a 33 year old woman who has had three consecutive first trimester losses at 8, 9 and 7 weeks, each with a foetal heart previously seen on ultrasound. She has no living children.

Her parental karyotypes are normal, her pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, and her thyroid function, prolactin and HbA1c are within normal limits. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on testing 14 weeks ago and again on repeat testing this week. Her anticardiolipin and beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies were negative on both occasions. She has never had a venous or arterial thrombosis, and has no rash or arthralgia. She has just had a positive home pregnancy test and her serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin today is 340 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 116/70, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive on two occasions 14 weeks apart; anticardiolipin and beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative; pelvic ultrasound normal cavity; parental karyotypes normal
data_table.Blood tests: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 340 IU/L; thyroid function, prolactin and HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for this pregnancy?

options.text: Low dose aspirin alone commenced today and continued until 36 weeks of gestation
options.rationale: Aspirin monotherapy gives a lower live birth rate than combination therapy in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome and is used only where heparin is contraindicated or declined (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Guidance; Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

options.text: Prednisolone with low dose aspirin commenced today and continued through the first trimester
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve live birth rates in this condition and add gestational diabetes, hypertension and preterm birth risk (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Guidance).

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin infusions given monthly through the first and second trimesters
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has not been shown to improve outcomes in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome and is not funded or recommended for this indication in Australia (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Guidance).

options.text: Vaginal progesterone pessaries nightly commenced today and continued until 16 weeks of gestation
options.rationale: Progesterone is considered for unexplained recurrent miscarriage with early pregnancy bleeding, which is a different indication from a confirmed antiphospholipid antibody (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Guidance).

options.text: Low dose aspirin with prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin commenced from today
options.rationale: Three consecutive first trimester losses with a persistently positive lupus anticoagulant meets criteria for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome, treated with aspirin plus prophylactic heparin from the positive pregnancy test, which raises live birth rates substantially (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Guidance; Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one treatable cause found in a substantial minority of recurrent miscarriage investigations, which is why it is tested for in every couple with three or more losses. Laboratory criteria require lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies positive on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, and a single positive result is not sufficient because transient antibodies follow infection. Clinical criteria are met by three or more consecutive losses before 10 weeks, one or more losses of a morphologically normal foetus after 10 weeks, or a preterm birth before 34 weeks for severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency. Treatment with aspirin and prophylactic heparin started as soon as pregnancy is confirmed raises live birth rates from roughly 10 per cent to around 70 per cent.
key_points: Two positive antibody results at least 12 weeks apart are required for diagnosis
Aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin is the treatment
Treatment starts at the positive pregnancy test rather than at the first scan
Corticosteroids and immunoglobulin do not improve outcomes and add risk
explanation.pearls: Lupus anticoagulant is the single antibody most strongly associated with adverse pregnancy outcome, and it cannot be interpreted while a woman is on heparin or warfarin, so testing must be completed before treatment starts.

subtopic_detail: Femoral fracture in a pre-ambulant infant with a normal bone profile
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a 3 month old boy brought in because he cries whenever his left leg is moved and his mother's partner noticed his thigh looked swollen this morning.

The history given is that he rolled from a lounge onto a carpeted floor yesterday afternoon, a distance of about 40 cm. He is not yet rolling or crawling according to his developmental history taken separately. Radiography shows a mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur. His sclerae are white, he has no joint hypermobility, his growth is along the 50th centile and there is no family history of fractures or hearing loss. His corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 78/46, RR 40, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Swollen left thigh with pain on movement; white sclerae; no joint hypermobility; no bruising elsewhere on exposed skin
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur; corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit, notify child protection services and arrange a skeletal survey with paediatric review
options.rationale: A femoral fracture in a pre-ambulant infant with a mechanism inconsistent with his developmental stage is highly suspicious for inflicted injury and mandates admission, statutory notification and a full skeletal survey (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse; Australian child protection mandatory reporting requirements).

options.text: Apply a hip spica cast and discharge with orthopaedic outpatient and general practitioner follow up
options.rationale: Treating the fracture alone returns the infant to an unassessed environment, and fracture management is never a substitute for the safety assessment (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey next week with a scheduled paediatric clinic appointment
options.rationale: Deferring the survey to an outpatient appointment is the near pair error, since it delays detection of other injuries and leaves the child unprotected in the interval (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Send genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta and defer notification until those results return
options.rationale: A normal bone profile with white sclerae, normal growth and no family history makes osteogenesis imperfecta unlikely, and genetic results take weeks while the statutory obligation to report a reasonable suspicion applies now (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

options.text: Discharge with analgesia and safety netting advice, with review by the child health nurse this week
options.rationale: Discharge without investigation or notification misses the substantial risk that further and more serious inflicted injury follows an unrecognised presenting injury (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse).

explanation.summary: Any fracture in a child who is not yet independently mobile carries a high probability of inflicted injury, and a femoral fracture in this age group is among the most specific presentations. The central assessment is whether the mechanism offered is plausible for the child's developmental stage and for the energy required to produce the injury, and a 40 cm fall onto carpet does not fracture a femur. Medical mimics such as osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets and metabolic bone disease are considered and are largely excluded here by normal biochemistry, normal sclerae, normal growth and an absent family history. Doctors in every Australian state and territory are mandated reporters, and the threshold for notification is a reasonable suspicion rather than diagnostic certainty.
key_points: Fractures in pre-ambulant infants are highly suspicious for inflicted injury
Assess whether the mechanism matches the child's developmental stage and the energy required
A skeletal survey is performed as an inpatient, not deferred to outpatients
The reporting threshold is reasonable suspicion, not diagnostic certainty
explanation.pearls: Repeat the skeletal survey at 11 to 14 days when inflicted injury is suspected; healing periosteal reaction and callus reveal rib and metaphyseal fractures that were invisible on the initial films.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Family Studies mandatory reporting guidance
